prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B012) at rank 1 and the optical lattice clock (B008) at rank 4, and the discussion has moved me to put B008 first. The lattice clock is a single, well-defined invention: Katori's magic-wavelength trapping, the demonstration of strontium lattice clocks, and Ye's group taking them to the 1e-18 level and into many-body clock physics. It is confirmed by independent laboratories across Sr, Yb and Hg, it is used in international comparisons, it supports relativistic geodesy and tests of fundamental constants, and it is the technical basis for the planned redefinition of the second. Attribution is the cleanest on the list: a two-person prize that maps onto proposal-and-first-realisation and record performance. It is also the candidate with the broadest independent support. All seven other members rank it in their top five and three place it first, from atomic theory, atomic experiment and applied experiment. That convergence comes from people who judged it on its merits, not only from my own taste. I do not equate this count with merit, but the underlying arguments hold up when I test them against my own field.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing and framing. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb and the 2012 prize covered ion control, so a committee must show that the lattice clock is a distinct achievement and not a continuation of those. The practical redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and one could argue the prize should wait for it, or that it will mean more once it does. There is also a credit question outside the two names: ion-clock groups and other strontium and ytterbium groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere pushed the field alongside JILA and Tokyo. I think the Katori and Ye pairing still captures the decisive credit, but it is a judgement and not a fact.

responses.point: The lattice clock removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms in parallel, so it is a decisive improvement in measurement accuracy, and the adjacent comb and ion-clock work is already honoured or separable.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and I now accept that the separation from 2005 and 2012 is clear enough. The comb gave the counting mechanism and the ion work gave single-particle control. The lattice clock's contribution is different: it combines a magic-wavelength trap with many atoms to gain stability and accuracy together. Where I qualify your view is that the pending redefinition of the second is not a reason to hurry. The achievement is already mature without it, so I do not want it to carry weight in our decision either way.

responses.point: Mehlig put trapped-ion quantum logic (B022) first and ranked the lattice clock fourth, treating it as a clean two-person invention, but placed it behind the Cirac-Zoller programme and its experimental realisation.
responses.response: I ranked B022 second myself, so I take the argument seriously: Cirac and Zoller defined how a quantum computer could be built, and that is a conceptual advance. My reservation is the experimental allocation. Wineland was honoured in 2012 for the underlying ion control, and the Innsbruck, NIST and other first-gate claims make Blatt's share contestable in a way that Katori's and Ye's are not. A trio in which one slot is disputed is a weaker prize than a pair with a clear split, so I would keep B022 as an alternative and not the lead, though I do not think it is far behind.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B035) first because the prediction was quantitative and the experiments were decisive, while the lattice clock sits fifth as a clean instrumentation advance.
responses.response: I agree that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by Jarillo-Herrero's discovery is a striking pairing and that the field is huge. My concern is maturity and attribution. Danielsson, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce all note that the origin of the superconductivity is still debated, and the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young and others) is not captured by the three names. I would not call that a flaw in the physics. It is a reason to prefer a result whose interpretation is settled, and I think the committee gains little by prizing a field before its central question is answered.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked the lattice clock first as an atomic-structure theorist and ranked circuit QED fourth, noting that circuit QED is distinct in subject from the 2025 prize but close in hardware and that Girvin, Huang and Devoret carry claims outside the three names.
responses.response: This is the point that changed my ranking. I opened with circuit QED, but you, Kroll, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce all flag how close it is to the 2025 recognition of superconducting circuits, and you also point out that Girvin and Huang sit outside the list. I think circuit QED is a distinct discovery, because strong coupling of an artificial atom to a resonator is not macroscopic quantum tunnelling, but I accept that a second circuit prize so soon, with a credit that is arguably incomplete, is harder to defend than the clock. I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Pearce, as an experimentalist, values the lattice clock as a measurement capability with broad downstream use, and ranked IceCube (B042) second as an instrumentation and discovery combination, while noting that IceCube's AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal predecessors have a legitimate claim.
responses.response: I share the view that the lattice clock is a measurement capability that others build on. On IceCube I agree that the detector is remarkable and that the diffuse flux is established, but I think your own reservation is the decisive one: the source identification rests on a handful of associations at modest significance, and the allocation to Halzen and Karle leaves real claims open. That makes it a less secure choice this year than the clock.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, or sees it as a continuation.
Whether the Katori and Ye pairing adequately covers the credit given the NIST, PTB, SYRTE and ion-clock contributions.
Whether a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon after 2025 would be accepted for circuit QED, given Girvin and Huang are outside the credited names.
Whether the redefinition of the second should affect timing in either direction.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents connections that bear on circuit QED (B012) and on superconducting-circuit work generally: I am director of WACQT at Chalmers, a close colleague of Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, a frequent co-author with Anton Frisk Kockum, and Chalmers hosted several researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I would flag these as possible grounds for recusal if B012 became the leading candidate. No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B008, B022 or the other shortlisted entries.
